name: Bias for Action
definition: Speed matters in business. Many decisions and actions are reversible and do not need extensive study. We value calculated risk-taking.

rows.situation: When the decision can be undone
rows.under: Studies it as if it were permanent. The window closes.
rows.justRight: Takes a calculated risk and moves. Checks whether it worked.
rows.over: Moves so fast that nobody can say what was decided, and undoing it costs more than deciding slowly would have.

rows.situation: When the decision is hard to undo
rows.under: Treats it like any other decision and rushes it.
rows.justRight: Slows down for the study the one-way door actually needs, then decides.
rows.over: Uses "one-way door" as a reason never to decide.

rows.situation: When the calendar is full of analysis
rows.under: Waits for a complete picture that will not arrive.
rows.justRight: Uses the data they have, picks the next reversible step, and goes.
rows.over: Equates motion with progress and starts three paths that nobody finishes.

rows.situation: When the next step has real downside
rows.under: Avoids the risk and the work stalls.
rows.justRight: Names the downside, takes the risk that is worth it, and watches the result.
rows.over: Takes the risk for the feeling of speed and skips the check that would have caught a bad call.

rows.situation: When someone asks for another round of study
rows.under: Agrees every time. Study becomes the product.
rows.justRight: Asks whether the study would change the next reversible step. If not, they move.
rows.over: Mocks the request for study even when the decision is a one-way door.
